title: From wanting to fight to wanting to know
hookLine: the Gita opens on armies wanting to fight, and turns when Arjuna asks to be taught
carry: jijnasa: the teaching begins when you ask to learn
tomorrow: who counts as 'my own people'? Arjuna asks.

cards: A blind king sits in his palace, far from the battle, and asks his advisor Sanjaya to tell him what's happening. That's how the Gita opens: not with God, not with a sermon, but with a worried father.
On the field of the Kurus, he asks, gathered there, wanting to fight, my sons and the sons of Pandu: what did they do, Sanjaya? Wanting to fight is one word, yuyutsavah. Not fighting yet.

teach.b: The line: dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah, mamakah pandavash chaiva kim akurvata sanjaya. Yuyutsavah grows from yudh, to fight.
Sanskrit can build a wanting-to form: the root's first sound doubles, and an s joins the end. Yudh becomes yuyuts-: wanting to fight. Now the same pattern somewhere very different.
The Brahma Sutras, a root text of Vedanta, open: athato brahmajijnasa. Now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman.
Jijnasa, from jna, to know: doubled sound, an s inside, wanting to know. And here's the teaching. The Gita itself travels from one wanting to the other.
Through chapter one, Arjuna argues: reasons not to fight, reasons the war is wrong.

teach.h: I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.
teach.b: Then, early in chapter two, he stops arguing and says to Krishna: I am your student. I have come to you; teach me. Shishyas te 'ham, shadhi mam tvam prapannam.
Only then does Krishna begin to teach.

teach.h: THE WISH TO KNOW COMES FIRST.
teach.b: That's how Hindu tradition says real learning starts: not with being right, but with the wish to know, and the humility to ask a teacher.
It's the spirit in which students traditionally bow to the guru before a lesson, and Vedanta's first line is a wish rather than an answer. The field is full of people wanting to fight.
The Gita happens because one man, for one moment, became a jijnasu, one who wants to know.

how: Some Hindus begin a reading of the Gita with its opening verse, dharmakshetre kurukshetre; students traditionally bow to the teacher or touch the book with respect before a lesson, and Vedanta study often begins with the Brahma Sutras' first line.

s: the Gita opens with Krishna speaking
it opens with a blind king asking what happened on the field.
Krishna starts teaching the moment the armies line up
he starts after Arjuna stops arguing and says, I am your student, teach me (2.7).
jijnasa and yuyutsu are built the same way
a doubled first sound and an s: wanting to know, wanting to fight.

games.q: a classmate says Hindus are just supposed to accept whatever they're told. from what you learned today, what's a fair reply?
o: 'Vedanta's first line is a wish to know, and the Gita starts when Arjuna asks to be taught.'
'the Gita says to win the argument first, then learn.'
games.why: athato brahmajijnasa: the wish to know Brahman opens the Brahma Sutras, and Arjuna's 'teach me' in 2.7 opens Krishna's teaching.

practice: Many Hindus begin study by touching the book with respect or saying a short prayer to the teacher. Try it: rest a hand on your heart, or on the book or screen in front of you, and say inside, teach me.
If you don't pray, name one thing you honestly want to understand this week, someone else's side included, and breathe with that wish for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Gita's first chapter: today, yuyutsavah, wanting to fight, from yudh, and its cousin form jijnasa, wanting to know. Same pattern, two roads, and the Gita takes the second.

orig.note: Sanskrit: yuyutsavah, those who want to fight, from yudh, to fight; Gita 1.1.

carryVoice: Your line: jijnasa, the teaching begins when you ask to learn. Arjuna stopped arguing and said, teach me. Chapter one, begun.
